A diode is **reverse biased** when its **anode** sits at a **lower** potential than its
**cathode**.
**Step 1 — state the test.** Read the diode symbol: the **triangle** is the anode (the p
side) and the **bar** is the cathode (the n side) ✓
forward: V_anode **>** V_cathode
reverse: V_anode **<** V_cathode ✓
**Step 2 — test each circuit.**
**(1)** anode at **5 V**, cathode earthed through the supply: anode higher →
**forward** ✗
**(2)** anode at **−20 V**, cathode at **−10 V**: −20 < −10, so the anode is
**lower** → **reverse biased** ✓
**(3)** anode at **15 V**, cathode at **10 V**: 15 > 10 → **forward** ✗
**(4)** anode at **20 V**, cathode at **−5 V**: 20 > −5 → **forward** ✗
**Step 3 — conclude.** Only the second circuit reverse-biases its diode ✓
**Why negative numbers trip people up.** −20 V is **lower** than −10 V ✓ The
comparison is of **potentials on the number line**, not of magnitudes. Reading "20" as
larger than "10" gives the wrong answer, and that is precisely the trap.
**What matters is the difference, not the absolute values.** Circuit 2 applies
V_anode − V_cathode = −20 − (−10) = **−10 V** ✓ a 10 V reverse bias. Both terminals
could be shifted by any amount and nothing would change.
**What reverse bias does.** It **widens** the depletion region and **raises** the
barrier ✓ Only a tiny leakage current of thermally generated minority carriers flows -
microamps or less - so the diode is effectively an **open switch**.
**What forward bias does.** It **narrows** the depletion region and **lowers** the
barrier ✓ Beyond about **0·7 V** for silicon the current rises steeply and the diode
behaves as a closed switch with a small fixed drop.
**The practical rule.** Current flows **in the direction the arrow points**, from the
triangle towards the bar ✓ and only then.
**Why this matters in circuits.** A diode is a one-way valve: it rectifies a.c.,
protects against reversed supplies, and clamps unwanted voltage swings ✓ Getting its
orientation right is the first step in reading any rectifier circuit.
∴ the second figure.

Arsenic is **pentavalent** and indium **trivalent**, so X is **n-type** and Y is
**p-type**; the battery's polarity then makes the junction **reverse** biased.
**Step 1 — classify the two dopants.**
**arsenic** - group 15, **pentavalent** ✓ a **donor**, so X is **n-type**
**indium** - group 13, **trivalent** ✓ an **acceptor**, so Y is **p-type**
**Step 2 — read the battery.** As connected in the figure, the supply makes the
**n** side (X) **positive** relative to the **p** side (Y) ✓
**Step 3 — classify the bias.** For a p-n junction,
forward: **p positive**, n negative ✓
reverse: **n positive**, p negative ✓
Here the n side is positive, so the junction is **reverse biased** ✓
**Step 4 — conclude.** **X is n-type, Y is p-type, and the junction is reverse
biased** ✓
**What happens inside under this bias.** The applied field **adds** to the built-in
field ✓ Electrons in the n region are pulled further right and holes in the p region
further left, both **away** from the junction - so the **depletion region widens** and
the barrier **rises**.
**The resulting current.** Only a tiny **leakage**, carried by thermally generated
minority carriers ✓ of order microamps in germanium and nanoamps in silicon, and almost
independent of the applied voltage.
**Why germanium leaks more than silicon.** Its band gap is **0·67 eV** against
silicon's **1·1 eV**, so many more carriers are generated thermally ✓ This is one
reason silicon displaced germanium in nearly all modern devices.
**Why doping with group 15 gives n-type.** The fifth valence electron finds no bond to
join and is held by only about **0·05 eV** ✓ Room temperature frees it, leaving a fixed
positive donor ion and a mobile **negative** carrier.
**Why group 13 gives p-type.** Only three bonds can be formed, leaving a **hole** which
accepts an electron from a neighbour and migrates as a mobile **positive** carrier ✓
**The crystal remains neutral throughout.** Each mobile carrier is balanced by a fixed
ion of opposite sign ✓ Only in the **depletion region**, where the mobile carriers have
left, does a net space charge appear - and that is what creates the barrier.
∴ X is n-type, Y is p-type and the junction is reverse biased.

Planck's constant has the dimensions of **angular momentum**.
**Step 1 — find the dimensions of h.** From E = hν:
[h] = [E]/[ν]
= [M L² T⁻²]/[T⁻¹]
= **[M L² T⁻¹]** ✓
**Step 2 — find the dimensions of angular momentum.** From L = mvr:
[L] = [M][L T⁻¹][L]
= **[M L² T⁻¹]** ✓
**Step 3 — conclude.** They match exactly ✓
**Why this is more than a coincidence.** Planck's constant **is** the natural quantum of
angular momentum ✓ In the Bohr model the electron's angular momentum is quantised as
L = n h/2π = **nℏ** ✓
and in quantum mechanics every angular momentum - orbital or spin - comes in multiples
or half-multiples of ℏ. The electron's spin is exactly **ℏ/2**.
**The units, read two ways.** The joule-second of Planck's constant is the same as the
kg m² s⁻¹ of angular momentum ✓
J s = (kg m² s⁻²)(s) = **kg m² s⁻¹** ✓
**Testing the other options.**
**Boltzmann constant** ✗ - energy per kelvin, [M L² T⁻² K⁻¹]
**force** ✗ - [M L T⁻²]
**linear momentum** ✗ - [M L T⁻¹], short by one power of length ✓
Only angular momentum matches all three exponents.
**The numerical values.**
h = **6·626 x 10⁻³⁴ J s** ✓
ℏ = h/2π = **1·055 x 10⁻³⁴ J s** ✓
Their extreme smallness is why quantisation is invisible in everyday rotation: a
spinning wheel carries some 10³⁴ units of ℏ, so the steps are utterly imperceptible.
**Other quantities sharing these dimensions.** **Action**, and the **angular impulse**
τΔt ✓ Indeed h is often called the **quantum of action**, and the path-integral
formulation of quantum mechanics rests on precisely that reading.
**A caution.** Sharing dimensions does not always mean sharing physical meaning - work
and torque are the classic counterexample ✓ Here, though, the identification is genuine
and is confirmed by the physics.
∴ angular momentum.

Air resistance depends on **shape**, and a streamlined body suffers least.
**Step 1 — recall the drag formula.**
F = ½ C_D ρ A v² ✓
With the cross-sectional area A, the density and the speed all the same, only the
**drag coefficient C_D** distinguishes the three bodies.
**Step 2 — rank the shapes by C_D.**
**disc**, flat face to the flow: C_D ≈ **1·1** - the largest ✓
**sphere**: C_D ≈ **0·47** ✓
**cigar-shaped** (streamlined teardrop): C_D ≈ **0·04** - the smallest ✓
**Step 3 — order the resistances.**
**3 < 2 < 1** ✓ the cigar least, the disc most.
**Why the flat disc is worst.** The air cannot flow smoothly around it ✓ It separates at
the sharp rim, leaving a wide **turbulent wake** of low pressure behind. The pressure
difference across the body is what the drag mostly consists of.
**Why the streamlined shape is best.** A long tapering tail lets the airflow close
behind the body **gradually**, with no separation and almost no wake ✓ A teardrop can
have less than a **tenth** the drag of a disc of the same frontal area - one of the most
dramatic results in fluid mechanics.
**Why the sphere lies between.** The front half is smooth, but the flow still separates
behind it, leaving a moderate wake ✓ Adding a tapering tail - turning it into a
teardrop - cuts the drag by an order of magnitude.
**The counter-intuitive detail.** A **rough** sphere can have **less** drag than a smooth
one at certain speeds ✓ The roughness trips the boundary layer into turbulence, which
clings to the surface longer and narrows the wake. This is exactly why a golf ball is
dimpled - and it flies nearly twice as far as a smooth one would.
**Why nature and engineering converge on the teardrop.** Fish, birds, aircraft
fuselages, submarines and airship hulls all approximate it ✓ It is the shape of least
resistance for motion through a fluid.
**Why the equal cross-sections matter.** The question removes **size** as a variable ✓
so the comparison is purely one of shape, which is exactly what C_D measures.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 < 2 < 3** ✗ reverses the order entirely. **2 < 3 < 1**
✗ and **3 < 1 < 2** ✗ misplace the sphere ✓ The disc must be the largest and the cigar
the smallest.
∴ 3 < 2 < 1.

Reflection at a denser medium introduces a **180° phase change**, which makes the
reflected and transmitted patterns complementary.
**Step 1 — follow the reflected light.** Two rays interfere: one reflected from the
**top** of the air film and one from the **bottom** ✓ The second reflects at a
glass surface - going from rarer to **denser** - and so suffers an extra phase change
of **π**, that is **180°** ✓
**Step 2 — see what that does at the point of contact.** The film thickness is zero
there, so the two rays have no path difference ✓ but the π phase change makes them
**destructive**, and the centre of the reflected pattern is **dark**.
**Step 3 — follow the transmitted light.** Both transmitted rays reflect internally at a
rarer medium, or not at all, so **neither** gains the extra π ✓ With no phase change
the centre is **bright**.
**Step 4 — conclude.** Wherever the reflected light is dark the transmitted is bright,
and vice versa ✓ Each colour missing from the reflection is present in the
transmission - the two are **complementary**, and the cause is the **180° phase change
in one of the reflected waves** ✓
**Why reflection at a denser medium inverts the wave.** It is the optical analogue of a
wave on a string reflecting from a **fixed** end ✓ The boundary condition forces the
reflected wave to be inverted; reflection from a **rarer** medium, like a free end,
produces no inversion.
**The condition for a dark ring in reflection.**
2µt = **nλ** ✓
and for a bright ring, 2µt = (n + ½)λ - the half-wavelength coming from the phase
change. In transmission the two conditions are **exchanged**.
**Why the centre is dark in reflection.** At t = 0 the condition 2µt = nλ is satisfied
with n = 0 ✓ This dark central spot is the standard test that the lens and plate are in
proper contact.
**Where the energy goes.** Nowhere - it is **redistributed** ✓ Light missing from the
reflected beam appears in the transmitted one, so energy is conserved overall. This is
true of all interference.
**The same principle elsewhere.** **Anti-reflection coatings** on lenses use a
quarter-wave layer so that the two reflections cancel ✓ and the colours of soap films
and oil slicks arise identically.
**Reading the distractors.** **90°**, **145°** and **45°** ✗ would give only partial
cancellation ✓ Complete complementarity requires exactly **180°**, which is what the
boundary condition at a denser medium provides.
∴ 180° change of phase in one of the reflected waves.

Work out the rotation **per centimetre** for each solution, then weight them by their
proportions in the mixture.
**Step 1 — find each solution's rotation per cm.**
first: 38°/20 cm = **+1·9° per cm** (right-handed, taken positive) ✓
second: 24°/30 cm = **−0·8° per cm** (left-handed, negative) ✓
**Step 2 — see what the 1 : 2 mixture contains.** In 30 cm of the mixture, one third is
the first solution and two thirds the second:
equivalent to **10 cm** of the first and **20 cm** of the second ✓
**Step 3 — add the contributions.**
from the first: 10 x (+1·9) = **+19°**
from the second: 20 x (−0·8) = **−16°** ✓
**Step 4 — total.**
19 − 16 = **+3°**
a **right-handed rotation of 3°** ✓
**Why the rotations simply add.** Optical rotation is **additive** over the path, and
each solute acts independently ✓ The dextrorotatory and laevorotatory contributions
subtract because they are opposite in sign - exactly as vectors along one line would.
**Why dilution matters.** Mixing halves or thirds the concentration of each component ✓
Since θ = Slc, the rotation per centimetre falls in the same proportion - which is why
the 1 : 2 ratio translates into 10 cm and 20 cm of equivalent path.
**A check by concentration.** Let the first solution have rotation constant k₁ = 1·9 and
the second k₂ = −0·8 per cm at full strength. In the mixture they are at 1/3 and 2/3
strength:
per cm: (1/3)(1·9) + (2/3)(−0·8) = 0·633 − 0·533 = **+0·1° per cm** ✓
over 30 cm: **+3°** ✓ the same answer.
**Why the result is small.** The two solutions nearly cancel ✓ The right-handed one is
stronger per unit length but present in smaller proportion, so only 3° of net rotation
survives from contributions of 19° and 16°.
**The sign convention.** Dextrorotatory (clockwise, seen looking towards the source) is
taken **positive**; laevorotatory **negative** ✓ Natural sucrose is dextrorotatory;
fructose is laevorotatory, which is why their mixture - invert sugar - rotates left.
**Reading the distractors.** **Left-handed 3°** ✗ has the sign wrong; the right-handed
contribution is the larger. **±14°** ✗ would follow from weighting the two equally or
from forgetting the dilution ✓
∴ right handed rotation of 3°.
